extracted.intended_audience: architects, architectural historians, students of art/architecture, and educated travellers interested in Venetian Gothic architecture
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing and identifying the characteristic forms, decorations, iconography, and functional decisions of Venetian Gothic palaces (with emphasis on the Ducal Palace and related domestic architecture). Useful for dating, stylistic attribution, and reproducing period-appropriate features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depiction of the months' labours in sculptural archivolts
rubrics_metrics.description: Months are represented by specific labours or activities appropriate to local climate and agricultural systems (e.g., June — reaping; July — mowing; August — threshing or gathering grapes in northern work; St Mark's has August asleep with the Virgin above).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sculptural programme varies by region — compare St. Mark's series with Northern manuscripts: where Northern work often shows threshing, vintaging, or sowing, Venetian/Italian versions may show different actions (e.g., August sitting with head on hand, Virgin above). The variations express the local climate and agricultural system and should be read comparatively (table of parallels provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Doorway arch forms and tympanum treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: In Venetian practice no 'arches of the fantastic fourth order' occur in doorways; the pure pointed arch appears earlier and more often in doorways than in window-heads; small early entrances are often square-headed without an arch, and the interval (tympanum) above the lintel is commonly filled with sculpture or closed by iron bars, sometimes with a projecting gable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are characteristic chronological/signature features: their presence or absence helps date and attribute doorways. The tympanum may carry shields, inscriptions or sculpture and the presence of a projecting gable/porch is typical in certain phases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Door-head sculpture subject matter (family shield and angelic protection)
rubrics_metrics.description: The door-head is commonly charged with the family shield or crest, protected by an angel; Venetian heraldry usually prefers angels as supporters rather than beasts, and an angel is often introduced above the shield bearing a globe (intended for the 'Angel of the Lord').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where elaborate sculpture is inadmissible the shield may be simply suspended by a leather thong and a cross introduced above the archivolt. Renaissance architects substituted heads of satyrs for crosses and angels — a clear stylistic shift and sign of period change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious inscription and benediction on doorways
rubrics_metrics.description: Early Venetian doorways typically bear the family name together with an intimation that the family places its defence and prosperity in God's hands, frequently accompanied by a general expression of benediction to the person passing the threshold (e.g., 'Peace be to this house', 'Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such inscriptions persist into the Renaissance in Venice; the presence, wording, or removal of these phrases is culturally and chronologically informative (the author notes modern Protestant aversion to such symbols).

rubrics_metrics.name: Central blessing motif (hand between sun and moon)
rubrics_metrics.description: A recurring motif in older Venetian work is the hand between the sun and moon in the attitude of blessing, expressing the general power and presence of God as the source of light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This motif is almost invariably found in the centre of the archivolt in older Venetian doorways and is diagnostic of that phase of work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of interior courts and wells
rubrics_metrics.description: Venetian palace gateways commonly lead into a long interior court, around which the palace mass is built; in the centre of the court there is almost always a marble well, often treated like a colossal capital with foliage at the angles and the family shield on its sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gothic wells from the thirteenth century onwards are numerous and typically similar in form; a surviving Byzantine example may be octagonal, treated like the richest Norman fonts. The well and court arrangement are essential for identifying Venetian domestic layout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design and sequencing of external staircases
rubrics_metrics.description: External staircases in Venetian palaces are often superb and sustained on four or five pointed arches that gradually increase in height and span as they ascend — a change in proportion noted as peculiar to Venice and a consequence of Byzantine façade practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These staircases are usually protected by exquisitely carved parapets, have lions or grotesque heads on the angles, and include projecting balconies on landing-places — details to look for when attributing or reproducing Venetian stair design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interior ceiling and colour decoration evolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Original interiors often had bold horizontal beams, richly carved and gilded; many Venetian interiors were later remodelled by Renaissance architects and covered with paintings by masters (Veronese, Titian, Tintoret) — a change in decorative system rather than mere loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author regards these remodellings favorably for their paintings; noting whether ceilings remain untouched or have later color decorations is important for period assessment and conservation decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritising interior function (illumination/comfort) over external symmetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Venetian Gothic practice sometimes deliberately sacrifices external symmetry to serve interior requirements (e.g., raising large windows to better light painted ceilings and to maintain a serene light inside a council chamber), which the author calls 'one of the most remarkable instances ... of the daring sacrifice of symmetry to convenience.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating façades, consider interior program — window placement may be driven by internal chamber needs (lighting paintings, comfort of assemblies) rather than external uniformity; such departures can be regarded as noble rather than defective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Façade composition: wall supported on tiers of shafts
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical façade composition in Venetian palaces: a smooth mass of wall sustained on two tiers of pillars/rows of shafts which carry the main walls; inner floors removed would leave a basilica-like form (two high walls on ranges of shafts roofed by a low gable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This simple structural arrangement explains fenestration and internal spatial effects and should be used as a diagnostic model when reading façades and internal stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and meaning of the term 'order' for grouped forms
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'order' is a useful word for any known group of forms (windows, capitals, bases, mouldings, etc.) provided it is not taken to imply preëminence or isolation; one may speak rationally of, e.g., the six orders of Venetian windows while allowing for many other distinguishable varieties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'order' as a classificatory convenience, but avoid implying a rigid hierarchy — stylistic description should remain flexible and comparative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stylistic layering as a dating criterion (Byzantine, Gothic, Renaissance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Ducal Palace (and Venetian architecture generally) often exhibits successive styles: Byzantine, Gothic, and Renaissance; the existing building is commonly a union of Gothic and Renaissance elements, and many details must be reviewed with documentary history to determine which parts belong to which period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of confused accounts and disputes among antiquaries about dating (e.g., whether a main façade is fourteenth or fifteenth century). Structural arrangement, decorative program, and documentary evidence must all be combined for reliable dating.
